CONCLUSIONS: This evidence calls attention to the importance of expectancies as a factor that may contribute to the understanding of individual differences in behavior under alcohol and a placebo.

screening.rationale: The study explicitly tested how expectancies predicted responses to both alcohol and a placebo (told-alcohol/got-placebo), making placebo response a primary focus (predictor of placebo-induced performance change).

classification.summary: Tested whether expected alcohol-induced impairment predicted motor performance; found that greater expected impairment predicted poorer performance under both alcohol and a placebo.
classification.key_finding: Found that higher expected impairment predicted poorer psychomotor performance under both 0.35 g/kg alcohol and told-alcohol/placebo sessions.

title: Conditioning allergic skin responses in humans: a controlled trial.
abstract: Classical conditioning of immune responsiveness has been extensively investigated in animals, but few successful studies have been reported with humans. We report the results of a study in which an attempt was made to demonstrate conditioned alteration to an allergic skin test response in humans. For 8 of 10 trials, allergic skin tests were administered to one forearm of volunteer subjects, and saline was administered to the other forearm. For the other two trials, the test substances were covertly switched between arms, but no changes in response resulted from this maneuver that could be ascribed to conditioning.

screening.rationale: Human experimental study tested classical conditioning of allergic skin responses (placebo/nocebo-relevant mechanism) with within-subject control, making conditioned immune response the explicit focus.

classification.summary: Tested classical conditioning of allergic skin-test responses in human volunteers using allergen versus saline on opposite forearms and found no conditioned alterations of the skin response.
classification.key_finding: No reliable conditioned change in allergic skin-test responses was observed.

title: Hypnotic analgesia, expectancy effects, and choice of design: a reexamination.
journal: The International journal of clinical and experimental hypnosis
abstract: Previous research by Stam and Spanos suggests that if waking analgesia is followed by hypnotic analgesia, subjects refrain from maximally responding during the waking trial so they report less pain under hypnosis (i.e., a "holdback effect"). This hypothesis was re-examined using more stringent controls. Thirty-six highly susceptible subjects chosen by a combination of the Harvard Group Scale of Hypnotic Susceptibility, Form A and the Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scale, Form C were randomly assigned to one of three treatment groups (waking analgesia followed by hypnotic analgesia, waking analgesia followed by waking analgesia, or hypnotic analgesia followed by waking analgesia). Each group received three 60-second immersions of cold pressor pain stimulation (baseline, Immersion 1, Immersion 2) and rated pain using a magnitude estimation and a category rating scale. The obtained results failed to support the hypotheses of a holdback effect or a "reverse-order holdback effect." Properties of within-subjects and between-subjects designs were considered in explaining the superiority of hypnotic analgesia over waking analgesia typically found in within-subjects models.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of hypnotic versus waking analgesia and tests of order/expectancy (holdback) made placebo/expectation effects and design choice the paper's explicit focus.

classification.summary: Randomized experiment in highly hypnotizable adults tested order and expectancy (holdback) effects comparing hypnotic versus waking analgesia during repeated cold-pressor immersions and found no support for the holdback hypotheses.
classification.key_finding: Did not find evidence of a holdback or reverse-order holdback effect; results discuss why within-subjects designs often show superiority of hypnotic analgesia.

title: Taped therapeutic suggestions and taped music as adjuncts in the care of coronary-artery-bypass patients.
journal: The American journal of clinical hypnosis
abstract: A randomized, single-blinded, placebo-controlled trial examined the benefits of taped therapeutic suggestions and taped music in coronary-artery-bypass patients. Sixty-six patients listened to either suggestion tapes or music tapes, intraoperatively and postoperatively; 29 patients listened to blank tapes intraoperatively and listened to no tapes postoperatively. Half the patients who listened to a tape found it helpful. There were no significant differences between groups in length of SICU or postoperative hospital stay, narcotic usage, nurse ratings of anxiety and progress, depression, activities of daily living, or cardiac symptoms. There were no significant differences in these same outcomes between the patients who were helped by the tapes and the patients not helped. These results suggest that if taped therapeutic suggestions have a measurable effect upon cardiac surgery patients, demonstrating this effect will require more detailed patient evaluations to identify subgroups of patients responsive to this type of intervention.

screening.rationale: Randomized, placebo-controlled trial explicitly tested taped therapeutic suggestions versus blank (placebo) tapes in CABG patients, making placebo/context effects the study focus.

classification.summary: Randomized single-blind trial tested taped therapeutic suggestions or music versus blank/no tapes in 66 CABG patients and found no significant differences in length of stay, narcotic use, anxiety, depression, or nurse-rated progress.
classification.key_finding: Found no significant benefit of taped therapeutic suggestions or music versus blank/no tapes on postoperative clinical and self-report outcomes.

title: Clinical response predictors in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of fluoxetine for geriatric major depression. Fluoxetine Collaborative Study Group.
abstract: BACKGROUND: We attempted to determine baseline characteristics predicting response in a 6-week, double-blind, geriatric depression trial, which showed a significantly higher remission rate for fluoxetine (20 mg daily) than for placebo (31.6% vs. 18.6%, p < .001). METHODS: Outpatients (N = 671) were 60 years or older (mean +/- SD = 67.7 +/- 5.7), met Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (3rd ed., rev., American Psychiatric Association, 1987) criteria for unipolar major depression, had baseline scores on the 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD17) of 16 or more, and were randomized after a 1-week placebo lead-in. Potential baseline predictors of percentage change in last-visit-carried-forward HAMD21 total scores were entered into a stepwise regression model. The sample was randomly divided into two groups (development and validation data sets) so that potential predictors could be confirmed in a second analysis. RESULTS: Of the 266 variables considered for their prognostic ability, 13 were found to be significant predictors using the development data set, including (a) presence of somatic complaints, absence of agitation, and presence of previous accidental injury for fluoxetine response; and (b) reported feelings of emptiness, absence of somatic complaints, and absence of early insomnia for placebo response. The second analysis using the validation data set failed to confirm statistical significance of predictors identified in the development data set. CONCLUSIONS: Although potentially useful baseline characteristics were initially identified as response predictors, conservative statistical methods failed to confirm any significant predictors of differential responses between fluoxetine and placebo in this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. These results suggest that response predictor analyses require confirmation before conclusions can be generalized.

screening.rationale: The study explicitly analyzed predictors of response separately for the placebo arm, making placebo response an analytic focus in a randomized, placebo-controlled trial.

classification.summary: Analyzed baseline predictors of response in a 6-week double-blind RCT of fluoxetine versus placebo in geriatric major depression and failed to confirm predictors of differential response, with placebo remission ~18.6%.
classification.key_finding: Identified candidate baseline predictors in a development sample but none were confirmed in validation; placebo remission rate was 18.6%.

title: Long-term habituation of brain evoked potential responses and pituitary-adrenal secretion with repeated (placebo) testing.
abstract: To study whether changes in late auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) and/or in stress-sensitive hormones of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) system take place between a first and a second placebo experiment and if so, whether these changes are possibly related to each other, we conducted two identical placebo sessions (2 ml 0.9% saline) and one cortisol session (50 mg) with 10 subjects on three different days. Plasma cortisol concentrations were significantly higher at the beginning of the first placebo experiment than the second, with a concordant decrease of plasma adrenocorticotropin hormone (ACTH) concentrations. In the AEP domain, a consistently lower P2 amplitude was observed in the first session. Since the change in late auditory processing could not be demonstrated after exogenous administration of cortisol, a direct mediation through an elevation of plasma cortisol concentrations or indirect mediation through a decrease of plasma ACTH concentrations seems unlikely. We rather propose that other stress-sensitive mechanisms, such as CCK, might account for the novelty-induced P2 amplitude lowering.

screening.rationale: Within-subject experiment examined physiological and neural changes across repeated placebo (saline) sessions, making placebo response/habituation the explicit focus.

classification.summary: Compared two identical saline (placebo) sessions and a cortisol session in 10 adults and found habituation: lower cortisol/ACTH and reduced auditory P2 amplitude in the second placebo session versus the first.
classification.key_finding: Plasma cortisol and ACTH levels and late auditory P2 amplitude decreased on the second placebo (saline) session relative to the first, indicating habituation of HPA and evoked-potential responses.

title: Evidence for the involvement of macrophage-derived nitric oxide in the immunomodulatory effect of morphine and aversive Pavlovian conditioning.
journal: Advances in experimental medicine and biology

screening.rationale: Title indicates an empirical study of Pavlovian (classical) conditioning producing immunomodulatory effects of morphine, which fits inclusion as mechanisms of conditioned placebo-like responses.

classification.summary: Provided evidence that macrophage-derived nitric oxide contributed to morphine's immunomodulatory effect and that aversive Pavlovian conditioning modulated immune responses.
classification.key_finding: Found that conditioned pairing involving morphine produced immunomodulation mediated in part by macrophage-derived nitric oxide.
